chapters.title: Unit 3: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
Unit 6: Market Failure and the Role of Government

terms.def: The ability to produce more of a good than another producer with the same resources, or the same amount with fewer resources.
Total revenue minus explicit costs, the money actually paid out to run the business.
Producing the quantity at which price equals marginal cost (P = MC), so the value buyers place on the last unit equals the cost of making it and total surplus is as large as it can be.
The space inside a shape on a graph: a rectangle's area is base × height and a triangle's is ½ × base × height, with the base read on the horizontal axis and the height on the vertical axis.
Average product: output per unit of an input, total product divided by the amount of that input (for labor, output per worker).
Average costs are costs per unit of output: average fixed cost (AFC = TFC / Q), average variable cost (AVC = TVC / Q) and average total cost (ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC).
Anything that keeps new firms from entering a market, such as a patent or license, control of a key resource, or economies of scale that give a large firm a lower average total cost.
The strategy that gives a player the largest payoff when the other player's choice is held fixed.
The limit a consumer's income and the prices of goods place on what can be bought: total spending cannot exceed the budget.
Latin for "other things equal": a curve shows how its two variables relate while everything else is held constant.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts and Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: A good that is excludable but nonrival, such as a streaming service or an uncrowded toll road. Firms can sell it because nonpayers can be kept out.

An agreement among rival firms to limit output or raise prices to increase their joint profit. A formal group that does this is a cartel; each member gains by cheating, so cartels tend to be unstable (and are illegal in many countries).
A good that is rival but nonexcludable, such as fish in open waters. Each user ignores the cost to others, so it is overused: the tragedy of the commons.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.

A constant-cost industry is one whose firms' costs do not change as the industry grows or shrinks, so its long-run supply curve is horizontal at minimum ATC. (Increasing- and decreasing-cost industries, whose costs rise or fall with industry size, are an extension.)

Consumer surplus (CS): the difference between what buyers are willing to pay and what they actually pay, summed over the units bought. On a graph, the area under demand and above the price, out to the quantity traded.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus

terms.def: A corrective (Pigouvian) tax or subsidy: a per-unit tax equal to the external cost, or per-unit subsidy equal to the external benefit, at the efficient quantity, which moves the market to MSB = MSC.

Cross-price elasticity of demand: the percent change in quantity demanded of one good divided by the percent change in the price of another. Positive for substitutes, negative for complements, near zero for unrelated goods.

Deadweight loss (DWL): the total surplus lost when the quantity traded differs from the efficient equilibrium quantity. On a graph, the triangle between demand and supply from the quantity traded to the equilibrium quantity.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: Demand: the quantities of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, shown as a downward-sloping demand curve. The quantity demanded is the amount at one particular price.
Demand for a factor of production that comes from the demand for the product it helps make. More demand for bread means more demand for bakers.

Determinants of demand: the changes other than the good's own price that shift demand: tastes, income (a normal good's demand rises with income, an inferior good's falls), prices of substitutes and complements, expectations and the number of buyers.

Determinants of price elasticity of demand: the availability of close substitutes, whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, its share of the buyer's budget, how narrowly the good is defined, and how much time buyers have to adjust.
A change other than the wage that shifts labor demand: the demand for the product, worker productivity, the prices of other inputs, or the number of firms.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in Factor Demand and Factor Supply

terms.def: Determinants of supply: the changes other than the good's own price that shift supply: input prices, technology, the prices of other goods the seller could produce, taxes and subsidies, expectations and the number of sellers.
Diminishing marginal returns: in the short run, as more of a variable input is added to a fixed input, the marginal product of that input eventually falls.
A direct (positive) relationship means two variables rise and fall together; an inverse (negative) relationship means one rises as the other falls.

A strategy that gives a player a higher payoff than its other strategies whatever the other player does; proved with one comparison for each of the other player's choices. A dominated strategy is one that another strategy always beats.
An increase in the most a producer or an economy can make, shown by an outward shift of the PPC, from more or better resources or better technology.
Total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs (accounting profit minus implicit costs). A negative economic profit is an economic loss.
The way a society answers the three questions scarcity forces: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
Economies of scale: long-run average total cost falls as the firm grows. Constant returns to scale: it stays flat. Diseconomies of scale: it rises as the firm grows.
In the long run, positive economic profit draws new firms into a market (entry) and economic losses push firms out (exit), shifting market supply until economic profit is zero.
terms.topicTitle: Firms' Short-Run Decisions to Produce and Long-Run Decisions to Enter or Exit a Market

terms.def: The gap between the output at the minimum of ATC and the smaller output a monopolistically competitive firm produces in long-run equilibrium, where its demand curve is tangent to the falling part of ATC.
A good is excludable when people who do not pay can be kept from using it (a concert with a ticket gate). It is nonexcludable when they cannot (national defense).

An explicit cost is a money payment for a resource, such as rent or wages paid; an implicit cost is the value of a resource the decision maker already owns or gives up, such as her own time, with no payment made.
A cost or benefit of producing or consuming a good that falls on people outside the market. Because buyers and sellers ignore it, the market quantity is not efficient.
A market where firms buy the factors of production (labor, land and capital) from the households that own them. The payments are wages, rent and interest.
The resources used to make goods and services: land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (tools, machines and buildings) and entrepreneurship (organizing and taking risks).
For a firm that sells every unit at one market price, the demand curve is a horizontal line at that price, and it is also the firm's marginal and average revenue: d = MR = AR = P.
The free-rider problem: people can enjoy a nonexcludable good without paying, so few pay and a market provides too little of it.
The study of choices when each player's payoff depends on the other players' choices (strategic interaction), used to model firms in an oligopoly.
A measure of inequality: the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve as a share of the whole triangle under the line. It runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1.
One of the two number lines of a graph: the horizontal axis (x-axis) runs left to right and the vertical axis (y-axis) runs up. On a market graph quantity goes across and price goes up.
Import quota: a legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported. It raises the domestic price and lowers imports as a tariff does, but raises no tariff revenue.

Imports: goods bought from other countries. At a world price below the domestic price, imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied. Exports are the reverse: at a world price above the domestic price, quantity supplied minus quantity demanded.
A reward or penalty that motivates a choice; in a market, a higher price is an incentive for firms to make more of a good.
Income effect: a lower price makes buyers' income go further, so they can buy more. Substitution effect: a lower price makes the good cheaper than its substitutes, so buyers switch toward it.

Income elasticity of demand: the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in income. Positive for a normal good (above 1 when demand grows faster than income), negative for an inferior good.
Income inequality is an unequal spread of yearly income across households; wealth inequality is an unequal spread of assets (savings, homes, businesses). Wealth earns income, so the two are linked.
Increasing opportunity cost means each extra unit of a good costs more of the other good, which bows the PPC out; constant cost gives a straight line and decreasing cost bows it in.
The point where two curves cross: the one price and quantity that lie on both curves.
The number of workers willing and able to work at each wage. It shifts with population, training and age rules, pay in other jobs and how people feel about the work.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in Factor Demand and Factor Supply

terms.def: The law of demand: other things equal, when a good's price rises the quantity demanded falls, and when it falls the quantity demanded rises.
The law of supply: other things equal, when a good's price rises the quantity supplied rises, and when it falls the quantity supplied falls.
A firm makes a given output at the lowest cost when the marginal product per dollar is the same for every input: MP of labor ÷ wage = MP of capital ÷ rental price.
terms.topicTitle: Profit-Maximizing Behavior in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets

terms.def: Long-run average total cost (LRATC): the lowest average total cost of producing each output when the firm can change every input, including its plant size.
In perfect competition, the state in which entry and exit have pushed the price to minimum ATC, so P = MR = MC = minimum ATC and every firm earns zero economic profit.

A curve that shows the cumulative percentage of income (or wealth) held by the cumulative percentage of households, ranked from lowest to highest. The diagonal line of equality shows perfectly equal shares.
A tax of a fixed amount that does not depend on how much a firm produces (a lump-sum subsidy is a fixed payment). It changes total fixed cost, AFC and ATC, but not marginal cost or AVC.
Marginal analysis decides one more unit at a time: do one more when its marginal benefit (the extra benefit of that unit) is at least its marginal cost (the extra cost of that unit).
Marginal cost (MC): the extra cost of doing one more unit of something, the change in total cost from one more unit. Keep going while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost (MB ≥ MC).
Marginal product (MP): the extra output from one more unit of an input, the change in total product divided by the change in that input.

Marginal resource cost (also marginal factor cost, MFC): the added cost of hiring one more unit of a factor, the change in total factor cost divided by the change in the quantity hired. For a wage taker it equals the wage.
terms.topicTitle: Profit-Maximizing Behavior in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets

terms.def: Marginal revenue (MR): the extra revenue from selling one more unit, the change in total revenue divided by the change in quantity.

For a firm with a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is less than the price after the first unit, because the price is cut on every unit sold; its MR curve lies below the demand curve (twice as steep when demand is a straight line).
Marginal revenue product: the extra revenue a firm earns from hiring one more unit of a factor. MRP = marginal product × marginal revenue (MP × P for a price taker).
Marginal social benefit (MSB) is the benefit of one more unit to everyone in society; marginal social cost (MSC) is its cost to everyone. The efficient quantity is where MSB = MSC.
terms.topicTitle: Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes

terms.def: The extra utility from consuming one more unit of a good (MU); it usually falls as more is consumed, which is diminishing marginal utility.
Marginal utility divided by the price of the good (MU/P). A consumer maximizes utility by spending the whole budget so that MU/P is equal across goods.
Market demand: the sum of every individual buyer's quantity demanded at each price (a horizontal sum of the individual demand curves).

A system in which households and firms make the main choices and prices coordinate them; in a command economy a central authority decides by plan, and a mixed economy combines markets with government rules and services.
Market equilibrium: the price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, where the demand and supply curves cross. The market clears at the equilibrium price.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus

terms.def: A market outcome that is not socially efficient: the market produces more or less than the quantity where MSB = MSC, leaving deadweight loss.
terms.topicTitle: Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes

terms.def: The ability of a firm to raise its price without losing all of its customers. A firm with market power is a price maker and faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
Market supply: the sum of every individual seller's quantity supplied at each price (a horizontal sum of the individual supply curves).

Midpoint method: a way to compute elasticity that divides each change by the average of the starting and ending values, so the answer is the same for a rise or a fall in price. One accepted route, not the only one.
Minimum efficient scale: the smallest output at which long-run average total cost reaches its lowest level.

A legal lowest wage. In a competitive labor market a binding minimum wage lowers employment; in a monopsony, one set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can raise both the wage and employment.
A market with many firms selling differentiated products (product differentiation: each version is a little different) and easy entry and exit. Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
A market with a single seller of a good with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry. The monopolist faces the whole downward-sloping market demand curve.
The surplus lost because a monopolist produces where MR = MC instead of where demand meets MC: the triangle between the demand curve and MC, from the monopoly quantity to the efficient quantity.
A market with a single buyer, most often one employer that hires nearly all the workers of a kind in an area. It faces the upward-sloping labor supply curve.
The wage a monopsonist pays: it hires where MRP = MFC and pays the wage read on the labor supply curve at that quantity. Its wage bill is that wage times the workers hired.
A move from one point to another on the same curve, caused by a change in a variable on one of the axes, such as the good's own price.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts and Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: An outcome in which each player's strategy is its best response to the other's, so neither player can gain by changing its strategy alone. A game can have one, several or no Nash equilibria (Nash equilibria) in pure strategies.

A market where one firm can supply the whole demand at a lower average total cost than two or more firms could, because ATC falls over the whole range of demand. Regulators may set the socially optimal price (P = MC, which leaves a loss) or the fair-return price (P = ATC, zero economic profit).

An external cost. From production it puts marginal social cost above marginal private cost (MPC); from consumption it puts marginal social benefit below marginal private benefit. The market makes too much.
Zero economic profit: revenue just covers every cost, explicit and implicit, so the owner earns exactly what her resources would earn in their next-best use.
A market with a few large firms, often protected by barriers to entry. Each firm's best choice depends on what its rivals do (interdependence).
The value of the next-best alternative given up when you make a choice; only the single next-best option counts.
Two numbers in parentheses, (x, y), that locate one point: the horizontal value first, then the vertical value.
A table of the payoffs (profits or other gains) each player gets from every combination of the two players' strategies. By convention the row player's payoff is listed first in each cell.

Per-unit subsidy: a payment from the government for each unit sold. It shifts supply down by the subsidy; buyers pay less, sellers receive more, and the cost to the government is the subsidy times the new, larger quantity.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: Per-unit (excise) tax: a fixed amount per unit sold. Collected from sellers, it shifts supply up by the tax; tax revenue is the tax times the quantity sold after the tax.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: A market with many buyers and sellers of an identical product, full information about prices and free entry and exit, so each firm is a price taker that cannot change the market price.

An external benefit. From consumption it puts marginal social benefit above marginal private benefit (MPB); from production it puts marginal social cost below marginal private cost. The market makes too little.
Price ceiling: a legal maximum price. It binds only below the equilibrium price, where it causes a shortage and only the quantity supplied at the ceiling is traded. Rent control is an example.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: Selling the same good to different buyers at different prices, for reasons other than differences in cost. It needs market power, a way to sort buyers and a way to stop resale. With perfect price discrimination each buyer pays the most they are willing to pay, so MR equals demand and output is where demand meets MC.

Price elasticity of demand: the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price, read as an absolute value. Elastic if greater than 1, inelastic if less than 1, unit elastic if 1; perfectly inelastic demand is vertical and perfectly elastic demand is horizontal.

Price elasticity of supply: the percent change in quantity supplied divided by the percent change in price (positive). Elastic supply (greater than 1) responds strongly; inelastic supply (less than 1) responds weakly; a vertical supply curve is perfectly inelastic.
Price floor: a legal minimum price. It binds only above the equilibrium price, where it causes a surplus and only the quantity demanded at the floor is traded.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: A game in which each player's dominant strategy leads to a Nash equilibrium that leaves both players worse off than if both had chosen differently (the prisoners' dilemma of two firms that both cut prices).

Producer surplus (PS): the difference between the price sellers receive and the least they would accept, summed over the units sold. On a graph, the area above supply and below the price, out to the quantity traded.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus

terms.def: The relationship between the inputs a firm uses and the most output it can make from them. In the short run at least one input is fixed; in the long run every input can change.
A production possibilities curve: a graph of every combination of two goods a producer can make when it uses all its resources efficiently with its current methods.
Making the most output possible from the resources available: any point on the PPC; a point inside it is inefficient.
A profit-maximizing firm hires a factor up to where its marginal revenue product equals its marginal resource cost (MRP = MRC). From a table: the last unit whose MRP is at least its MRC.
terms.topicTitle: Profit-Maximizing Behavior in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets

terms.def: Produce the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC); from a table, the last unit whose MR is at least its MC.
A tax that takes a larger share of income as income rises. A proportional tax takes the same share from all incomes; a regressive tax takes a larger share of lower incomes.
Legal rights to own, use, sell and gain from property such as land, buildings and businesses; secure private property gives owners a reason to produce and invest.
A good that is both nonrival and nonexcludable, such as national defense or a flood wall. A private good is rival and excludable.
Quantity control (quota): a legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be sold. A binding quota holds the quantity below equilibrium, which raises the price and creates a deadweight loss.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: Regulation of market power: government policies, such as price ceilings on a monopoly and fair-return or socially optimal pricing of a natural monopoly, that move a firm with market power toward more output at a lower price.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Different Market Structures

terms.def: How output responds when every input grows by the same share. If inputs double and output more than doubles, increasing returns to scale; exactly doubles, constant; less than doubles, decreasing returns to scale.
A good is rival when one person's use leaves less for others (a sandwich). It is nonrival when many can use it at once without reducing each other's use (a radio broadcast).
The basic problem that resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so people, firms and governments must choose.
A move of the whole curve to a new position, caused by a change in something other than the two graphed variables; right means a larger quantity at every price, left a smaller one.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts and Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: Shortage (excess demand): at a price below equilibrium, the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. It pushes the price up.
terms.topicTitle: Market Disequilibrium and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: In the short run, a firm produces where MR = MC as long as the price is at least the lowest point of average variable cost; below that price (the shutdown point) it shuts down and loses only its fixed cost.
terms.topicTitle: Firms' Short-Run Decisions to Produce and Long-Run Decisions to Enter or Exit a Market

terms.def: Simultaneous shifts: demand and supply shifting at the same time. The change both shifts agree on is certain; the other is indeterminate, meaning it depends on which shift is larger.
terms.topicTitle: Market Disequilibrium and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: How steeply a line rises or falls: the rise (change in the vertical value) divided by the run (change in the horizontal value).
Concentrating production on the goods a producer makes at the lowest opportunity cost, and trading for the rest.
A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered; it is the same whatever is chosen next, so it does not change the best decision.
Supply: the quantities of a good sellers are willing and able to offer at each price, shown as an upward-sloping supply curve. The quantity supplied is the amount offered at one particular price.

Surplus of a good (excess supply): at a price above equilibrium, the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. It pushes the price down. Not the same as consumer or producer surplus.
terms.topicTitle: Market Disequilibrium and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: Tariff: a tax on imports, per unit. It raises the domestic price by the tariff, raises domestic output, cuts imports and creates deadweight loss. Tariff revenue is the tariff times the imports after the tariff.

Tax incidence: how the burden of a tax is shared between buyers (the rise in the price they pay) and sellers (the fall in the price they keep). The less elastic side bears more, whoever hands the tax to the government.
terms.topicTitle: The Effects of Government Intervention in Markets

terms.def: The rate at which one good is exchanged for another; trade benefits both sides when the terms lie between their opportunity costs, and those benefits are the gains from trade.
Everything a choice gives the decision maker: satisfaction for a consumer, revenue for a firm. Net benefit is total benefit minus total cost.

Total cost: everything a choice costs, its explicit costs (money paid out) and its implicit costs (the value of the next best alternative given up). A choice is worth making when total benefit exceeds total cost.
Total fixed cost (TFC): a cost that does not change with output in the short run, such as rent, and that is paid even when output is zero.
Total product (TP): the whole amount of output a firm produces with a given amount of an input, such as a number of workers.

Total revenue (TR): price times quantity sold. The total revenue test: with elastic demand, price and TR move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand they move together; with unit elastic demand TR does not change.
Total surplus: consumer surplus plus producer surplus, the total gain from trade in a market. In a competitive market it is largest at the equilibrium quantity.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium and Consumer and Producer Surplus

terms.def: Total variable cost (TVC): a cost that rises and falls with output, such as materials and hourly labor; it is zero when output is zero.
Giving up some of one thing to get more of another; every choice under scarcity involves one.
A payment from the government, such as cash aid to low-income households, for which no good or service is given in return.
A curve that falls, reaches a minimum point where its slope is 0, and then rises.
The satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming goods and services; total utility is the satisfaction from all the units consumed.
A firm that hires so small a share of a labor market that it takes the market wage as given; its labor supply line is horizontal at that wage (S = MFC = W).
terms.topicTitle: Profit-Maximizing Behavior in Perfectly Competitive Factor Markets

terms.def: World price: the price of a good on the world market. A small country that opens to free trade takes it as given, so its domestic price moves to the world price.
